system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 15 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2146-07-14 06:13:00 to 2146-07-28 11:20:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with abdominal pain, fever, and cloudy urine, two weeks after a prior hospitalization for pyelonephritis. He has a history of neurogenic bladder with a urostomy and a left nephrostomy tube due to ureteral stricture and severe hydronephrosis. He was diagnosed with acute pyelonephritis caused by Escherichia coli, with acute kidney injury on stage IV CKD and hyponatremia. He was started on empiric IV antibiotics, later transitioned to ertapenem via a newly placed PICC line. His infection resolved, renal function improved, and electrolytes stabilized. He was discharged home with home health services to complete a three-week course of IV antibiotics, with follow-up planned in urology, nephrology, and primary care, including nephrostomy tube management and monitoring of a lung nodule.
problems: Acute pyelonephritis without lesion of renal medullary necrosis
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage I through stage IV, or unspecified
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy
Other artificial opening of urinary tract status

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. You were admitted last night with fever and multiple wounds. Can you tell me how you've been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning, doc. I’ve been feeling awful—fever, chills, and my back and hip sores are really bad. I noticed a new one on my right hip just yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And the sore on your left foot—how long has that been there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About two weeks. I fell out of my chair and hurt it. It got worse, then I bumped it again a few days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And you mentioned feeling like you have a UTI—more sediment in your urostomy bag?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, more gunk than usual. But no flank pain, and my nephrostomy tube is draining clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. We ran some labs. Your white blood cell count is high—16.5—so your body is fighting an infection. We also saw your creatinine is up to 4.0, which is a bit high for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, my kidneys have always been weak. But is the infection from the sores or the urine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, we think the sores are the main source. The fever, high white count, and the foul smell from your sacral wound point to that. But we did get a urine culture to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve had so many UTIs before. I just don’t want it to turn into sepsis again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re already treating you for sepsis. You’re on IV daptomycin and meropenem—strong antibiotics. The wound team and plastic surgery are involved too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Meropenem? I’ve had bad reactions to some antibiotics before. Are you sure this is safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we checked your allergies. You’re not allergic to meropenem. It covers the bacteria we’re worried about, especially with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. What about my foot? The X-ray didn’t show a fracture, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. The X-ray shows severe osteopenia and soft tissue swelling, but no fracture. We did a small biopsy today to check for infection or other issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that tell us if it’s infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It will help. The initial report says no bacteria or fungi were seen, but we’re still waiting on final cultures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative—no bacteria in the blood. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the infection isn’t spreading?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not through your bloodstream, which is great. But your wounds are still infected. The plastic surgery team will do a bedside debridement today to clean out the dead tissue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you pain medication beforehand. It’s important to remove the dead tissue so the wound can heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. ___. How are you feeling after yesterday’s procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sore, but better. The wound feels cleaner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re going to repeat the debridement every few days. The tissue culture from your foot didn’t grow anything, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ulcer is likely from trauma and pressure, not deep infection. But we’re still treating the other wounds aggressively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back. You have both E. coli and Klebsiella growing in high numbers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no—is that why I’m so sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but you often carry these bacteria. Given your fever and wounds, we think the skin infections are the main issue. The antibiotics you're on cover both organisms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doc, I’ve been feeling weak. Is it the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your labs. Your potassium was high—5.7—yesterday. You refused treatment, but your repeat level is normal now. You said you’d drink more water and avoid juice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been doing that. Didn’t want an IV or monitors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. Just keep it up. Your kidney function is stable now—creatinine down to 3.2.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another debridement yesterday. The wound is looking cleaner. Plastic surgery thinks you’re healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the MRI they wanted for my hip?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You declined it, and the team agrees it’s not urgent. They don’t think the infection has reached the bone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My nephrostomy stitch came loose the other day. Is that a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we fixed it. You declined a follow-up X-ray, so we placed a stat lock to secure the tube. Just watch for any leakage or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another debridement done. Your wounds are improving. We’re on day 8 of antibiotics—two more weeks planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get them at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, through a PICC line. Infectious disease will follow up with you as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been thinking about that lung nodule from last year. Should I get the CT scan now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s recommended, but you declined during this admission. Please schedule it soon as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your white count is down to 11, and you’ve been fever-free for 48 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly by the end of the week. We’ll keep the antibiotics going and make sure your wounds are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I heard something about cocaine in my test. I used it once a while ago. Is that a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s important to avoid it, especially with your heart and kidney issues. We recommend counseling to help with cessation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is now 3.0—back to your baseline. That’s excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my pain meds? I’m on 60 mg oxycodone at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to 10 mg as needed for now. We want to avoid over-sedation. You’ll go back to your usual dose at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve arranged for an alternating pressure mattress to be delivered to your home to prevent future sores.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. My old one popped last month. That’s probably why my sores got worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What follow-ups do I need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Plastic surgery to monitor your wounds, urology and nephrology for your kidneys and tubes, and infectious disease for your antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lung scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please schedule that too. And keep taking your other medications as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. We’ll send your prescriptions and equipment order with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with fever, sepsis, and multiple infected pressure ulcers on the sacral region and right hip, along with a traumatic ulcer on the left foot. He was started on IV daptomycin and meropenem for broad-spectrum coverage. The wound care and plastic surgery teams performed several bedside debridements. Although urine cultures grew E. coli and Klebsiella, the source of sepsis was attributed to the skin wounds. He developed transient hyperkalemia, which resolved with hydration. His nephrostomy stitch dislodged during admission and was secured with a stat lock. He completed a two-week antibiotic course and was discharged home with a new pressure-relief mattress, follow-up planned with plastic surgery, urology, nephrology, and infectious disease, and instructions to complete outpatient imaging for a known lung nodule.
